chief_complaint: bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever for 2 weeks
hpi_details: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever for 2 weeks. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she caught a severe bacterial stomach bug from some undercooked takeout food she ate two weeks ago.
concerns: She is worried that passing blood in her stool means she has developed colon cancer like her aunt who passed away.
expectations: She hopes to have her stool tested and be prescribed strong antibiotics to clear up whatever infection is causing the bleeding.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ulcerative Colitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes assessing severity, obtaining stool testing to exclude infection, and arranging endoscopy with biopsies to confirm the diagnosis before starting mesalamine or corticosteroids, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever for 2 weeks

Key HPI features: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever for 2 weeks. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Ulcerative Colitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ulcerative Colitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Crohn's disease without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever with bloody diarrhoea for two weeks — raises concern for severe or fulminant colitis.
management_principles: Evaluate the severity of bloody diarrhea, obtain stool testing including C. difficile when indicated, and confirm inflammatory bowel disease with endoscopy/biopsies before immunosuppression unless a specialist directs urgent treatment
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 32F presents with a 2-week history of bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and fever, raising concern for inflammatory bowel disease versus infectious colitis.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Ulcerative Colitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Inflammatory colitis, including ulcerative colitis, is possible; infectious colitis and disease severity require prompt evaluation before immunosuppressive treatment.
reference_soap.plan: Assess severity and hydration status, obtain stool testing including C. difficile when indicated, and arrange Gastroenterology evaluation with endoscopy and biopsies to confirm inflammatory bowel disease. Do not start corticosteroids before infectious causes are reasonably excluded unless a specialist directs urgent treatment. Escalate urgently for systemic toxicity, severe abdominal pain/distension, or inability to maintain hydration.

teaching.one_liner: Autoimmune inflammation limited to the colon lining causes continuous bloody diarrhoea, cramping, and fever, usually starting in the rectum and spreading upward.
red_flags: Fever with bloody diarrhoea for two weeks — raises concern for severe or fulminant colitis

must_ask.say: Is there blood mixed into every bowel movement?
How many times a day are you passing bloody stool?
Have you had a fever along with the diarrhoea?
Do you feel a sudden urgent need to go, even with little warning?
Does it wake you up at night to go?
Have you lost any weight recently?
Does anyone in your family have Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis?

history.answer: I have been having frequent bloody diarrhea and lower belly cramping for the past two weeks, and I've also been feeling feverish.
It started about two weeks ago and has been gradually getting worse each day.
I go to the bathroom about six to eight times a day, and the stools are mostly loose and watery with bright red blood mixed in.
Yes, there is bright red blood mixed with slime or mucus almost every time I go.
Yes, I wake up two or three times every night with sudden urges to run to the toilet.
It is a crampy pain mostly in my lower belly on the left side, which gets a little better right after I have a bowel movement.
Yes, I constantly feel an urgent need to empty my bowels, but when I sit down, sometimes only a little bloody mucus comes out.
I have had a low-grade fever on and off for the past two weeks with occasional chills, and I feel worn out.
I feel mildly nauseated because of the cramps, but I haven't thrown up.
My mouth feels quite dry and I feel a little lightheaded when I stand up quickly, though I am still drinking water.
No, I haven't eaten any raw fish, undercooked meat, or buffet food, and my family eats the same food and feels completely fine.
No, I haven't traveled anywhere outside the city or gone camping recently.
No, I haven't taken any antibiotics in the past year, and I haven't started any new prescriptions or been hospitalized.
I have lost about two kilograms over the last two weeks because my appetite has dropped and eating triggers the cramping.
No specific food seems to cause it, and cutting out milk or bread hasn't made any difference.
I do have some work stress, but this is nothing like regular nervousness and I don't alternate with constipation.
No, I haven't noticed any joint pain, skin rashes, mouth sores, or red, painful eyes.
No, I don't have heart palpitations, heat intolerance, or sudden facial flushing.
I thought maybe I picked up a bad food bug from some takeout I had right before all this started.
Seeing all that blood really terrifies me because my aunt died of colon cancer and I'm scared it's happening to me.
I was hoping to get my stool checked and get some strong antibiotics to knock out this infection right away.
I have always been healthy and have never had chronic illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or bowel problems before.
I have never had any surgeries or prior hospital stays.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter pain pills, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medicines.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink a glass of wine or beer socially once or twice a month, but I haven't touched any alcohol since this started.
I work as an office administrator and live with my husband in an apartment.
My mother has mild high blood pressure, but no one in my family has Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or bowel cancer.
My last period started three weeks ago and came on time, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 115/75 mmHg, pulse 90 bpm, temperature 38.0 C, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, SpO2 99% on room air.
Mild conjunctival pallor without scleral icterus; no conjunctival injection.
Slightly dry oral mucosa without aphthous ulcers or thrush.
Flat, non-distended abdomen with no surgical scars or dilated veins.
Hyperactive bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants.
Mild to moderate tenderness on palpation over the left lower quadrant and hypogastrium without guarding.
No rebound tenderness elicited in any quadrant.
No perianal fissures, skin tags, or fistulae; digital examination reveals mild rectal tenderness with fresh blood and mucus on the examining glove.
No peripheral joint erythema, swelling, or limitation of motion in the knees, ankles, or wrists.
Decreased skin turgor consistent with mild dehydration; no erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, or purpura.
